properties.line: Denver & Rio Grande: Royal Gorge Route (Denver – Pueblo – Tennessee Pass – Grand Junction)
properties.speed_source: estimated for a heavy-grade mountain main line (Tennessee Pass, at over 10,200 ft, was the highest mainline rail crossing in the US) with sharp curves through the Royal Gorge, Eagle River, and Glenwood Canyons; unsourced

segments.note: The railroad standard-gauged and built the more direct Tennessee Pass line (Leadville-Pando-Glenwood Springs, cresting at 10,239 ft, the highest mainline crossing in the US) by 1890, superseding the old Marshall Pass route (see drg_marshall_pass_black_canyon.geojson for that earlier alignment) as the through main line: Denver - Colorado Springs - Pueblo - up the Arkansas River through the Royal Gorge to Salida - over Tennessee Pass - down the Eagle and Colorado Rivers through Glenwood Canyon to Grand Junction. Marketed as the 'Royal Gorge Route.' Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Colorado portion (Denver area - Colorado Springs - Pueblo - Royal Gorge - Salida - Tennessee Pass - Glenwood Canyon - Grand Junction) of a real-traced 854-point OpenStreetMap route, split at the Colorado-Utah state line (~index 539 of the original combined trace) so the Utah portion can carry its own company history (Rio Grande Western Railway was a legally separate company until 1908). No leg is a straight-line placeholder. FIXED 2026-08-24: this feature previously had a segment asserting service 1882-1890 over this exact alignment, but the note attached to that segment itself said the real 1882 route to Grand Junction went via Marshall Pass/Gunnison/Montrose, 'not the route shown here' -- the Tennessee Pass alignment traced here did not exist until 1890. That segment has been removed; 1882-1890 service is now drawn separately in data/drg_marshall_pass_black_canyon.geojson over its own, correct alignment. Straight-line repair 2026-08-29: 3 ruled segments totalling 40 mi replaced with OpenStreetMap-traced rail geometry (see geometry_repairs for the OSM lines each one followed).

properties.company: Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad
properties.line: Denver and Rio Grande Western: Royal Gorge Route / Scenic Limited
properties.speed_source: estimated for a heavy-grade mountain main line (Tennessee Pass, at over 10,200 ft, was the highest mainline rail crossing in the US) with sharp curves through the Royal Gorge, Eagle River, and Glenwood Canyons; unsourced

segments.note: D&RGW took formal control Aug 1, 1921 after the D&RG's bankruptcy reorganization -- old D&RG stockholders received nothing from the new company, a genuine change of ownership, not just a rename, so this feature is colored separately from the preceding D&RG era. The Scenic Limited was the flagship train on this route by the early 20th century. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

The Scenic Limited continued running via the Royal Gorge/Tennessee Pass route even after the Moffat Tunnel route opened, though it was increasingly overshadowed by faster Moffat Tunnel trains. Frequency estimated, unsourced.
The Scenic Limited was replaced by the Royal Gorge on June 2 1946. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

Declining patronage led the Royal Gorge to be cut back to a Denver-Salida turn on Dec 6 1964, no longer reaching Grand Junction. The last run of the train was July 27 1967, ending regular passenger service over this route -- Amtrak's 1971 network never served it, having inherited the Moffat Tunnel route instead. Today the line is owned by Union Pacific (via the 1988 D&RGW/Southern Pacific merger and 1996 SP/UP merger); the Tennessee Pass segment specifically has been mothballed and out of service since 1997, though UP has studied reactivating it for freight capacity. This feature traces the historic passenger-era route, not current active trackage.

properties.line: Rio Grande Western: Grand Junction – Salt Lake City
properties.speed_source: estimated for a heavy-grade mountain main line (Tennessee Pass, at over 10,200 ft, was the highest mainline rail crossing in the US) with sharp curves through the Royal Gorge, Eagle River, and Glenwood Canyons; unsourced

segments.note: Organized July 21, 1881 as the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railway (a legally separate company from the Denver & Rio Grande, despite the confusingly similar name -- and not to be confused with the 1921 Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad, a different company four decades later that happened to reuse a near-identical name). Built west from the Colorado line via Green River and Price toward Salt Lake City; its construction crews met the D&RG's, building west from Grand Junction, a few miles west of Green River on March 30, 1883, completing a through narrow-gauge Denver-Salt Lake City route. Reorganized and renamed the Rio Grande Western Railway in 1889 (consolidating with the State Line and Denver Railway); George Gould took stock control in Feb 1901, then formally merged it into the Denver & Rio Grande on Aug 1, 1908, ending its separate corporate existence -- the split used here follows this dataset's convention of coloring by the formal merger since, unlike some of this project's other splits, no source found describes D&RG actually dispatching or staffing RGW's trains before 1908, only holding its stock from 1901. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.line: Denver & Rio Grande: Grand Junction – Salt Lake City
properties.speed_source: estimated for a heavy-grade mountain main line (Tennessee Pass, at over 10,200 ft, was the highest mainline rail crossing in the US) with sharp curves through the Royal Gorge, Eagle River, and Glenwood Canyons; unsourced

segments.note: The Rio Grande Western Railway was formally merged into the Denver & Rio Grande Railroad (reincorporated as "Denver & Rio Grande Railroad (Consolidated)") on Aug 1, 1908, together with several smaller Utah subsidiaries, unifying the Denver-Salt Lake City route under one company for the first time. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.company: Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad
properties.line: Denver and Rio Grande Western: Grand Junction – Salt Lake City
properties.speed_source: estimated for a heavy-grade mountain main line (Tennessee Pass, at over 10,200 ft, was the highest mainline rail crossing in the US) with sharp curves through the Royal Gorge, Eagle River, and Glenwood Canyons; unsourced

segments.note: D&RGW took formal control Aug 1, 1921, the same genuine-ownership-change reorganization noted on the Colorado portion. This Grand Junction-Salt Lake City trackage carried the Scenic Limited/Royal Gorge (via the Colorado portion above) and, from 1934, also connected at Dotsero to the new Moffat Tunnel route. In 1949 it became the Utah leg of the jointly branded California Zephyr (Chicago, Burlington & Quincy / Denver & Rio Grande Western / Western Pacific) -- drawn here only through 1949; see california_zephyr_historical.geojson for the Zephyr-era service that continued over this same trackage afterward, through Amtrak's takeover in 1983 and to the present day. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

metadata.note: RESTRUCTURED 2026-08-24: this file used to be a single feature spanning Denver to Salt Lake City, colored 'Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad' for its entire 1882-1967 span even though that company name didn't exist until 1921, and even though a large western portion (Grand Junction-Salt Lake City) was run by the legally separate Rio Grande Western Railway until 1908. It's now six features: the Colorado portion split D&RG (1890-1921)/D&RGW (1921-1967), and the Utah portion split RGW (1883-1908)/D&RG (1908-1921)/D&RGW (1921-1949, handing off to california_zephyr_historical.geojson thereafter). The 1882-1890 segment previously on the Colorado portion, which the note itself flagged as the wrong alignment for those years, has been removed and is now correctly drawn in data/drg_marshall_pass_black_canyon.geojson.
